title: World consumption
question: Where do estimated consumption levels differ geographically?
reading: Country colours reveal geographic patterns; land area does not represent population or alcohol volume.
reason: A choropleth places consumption estimates in their geographic context, making broad spatial patterns visible.
alternative: Ranked bars would compare country values more precisely but would hide their geographic arrangement.
limitation: Large countries attract more visual attention. Grey means no matched estimate, not zero consumption.

title: Regional drinking distributions
question: How variable are country estimates within each region, and where does Australia sit?
reading: Boxes show regional variation that an average would conceal; the outlined diamond identifies Australia.
reason: Boxplots summarise the median, middle half and full range of many country estimates without a crowded list.
alternative: Regional average bars would conceal how different the countries within a region can be.
limitation: Each country has equal weight. Whiskers show the minimum and maximum, not the usual 1.5-IQR rule; country counts and quartiles are in the tooltip.

title: Six decades of availability
question: How did Australian alcohol availability change over time?
reading: The connected line makes long-term peaks, turning points and recent changes easier to follow than separate annual bars.
reason: Position on one time axis supports reading a continuous trajectory across six decades.
alternative: Annual bars would emphasise individual years and make the overall path harder to follow.
limitation: Availability measures supply per person aged 15+, not an individual's reported intake.

title: Beverage composition
question: How has the composition of available pure alcohol changed?
reading: Stacked bands keep the whole at 100% while showing how the beverage mix changes over time.
reason: A 100% stacked area chart communicates composition and change together. The main latest-year shares are directly labelled.
alternative: Separate lines would make individual trajectories easier to compare but weaken the immediate part-to-whole reading.
limitation: Middle bands do not have a common baseline. Hover for exact shares, including cider's small share; these are pure-alcohol shares, not beverage-volume shares.

title: Age and survey waves
question: Which age groups report higher percentages, and how does the pattern differ across survey waves?
reading: The age-by-year grid exposes patterns without overlapping many lines; darker cells always mean higher percentages.
reason: A heatmap fits many age-by-wave combinations into a readable matrix with chronological columns and ordered age groups.
alternative: Multiple lines would help trace one group precisely but become crowded when all groups are shown.
limitation: The 0–60% scale stays fixed across measures. Blank cells are missing or unsuitable estimates, and each wave samples different people.

title: Adolescent drinking
question: What does the selected reported percentage look like out of 100 percentage points?
reading: The grid explains one selected share out of 100 percentage points; the large number preserves the exact estimate.
reason: A waffle supports a focused, accessible part-to-whole explanation of one selected group and drinking period.
alternative: A bar would be more compact and better for simultaneous comparison of many categories.
limitation: Squares are percentage points, not individual students. A fractional square preserves the published decimal estimate.

title: Adult gender gap
question: How large is the male–female difference within each adult age group?
reading: Connectors expose each age group's gap: teal circles show males and plum squares show females.
reason: Two connected positions on the same percentage axis make within-age differences visible with little visual clutter.
alternative: Grouped bars would work, but the distance between estimates is less explicit.
limitation: These are source-specific survey estimates. Differences describe association, not a causal explanation.

title: Overlapping thresholds
question: How do weekly volume and monthly high-volume occasions overlap?
reading: Columns separate weekly volume; within drinker columns, lower cells represent monthly high-volume occasions. Areas show population shares.
reason: A mosaic represents the joint structure of two thresholds as well as the five category shares. Abstainers are separate.
alternative: A pie or a single stacked bar would show category shares without making the two-threshold organisation as explicit.
limitation: Cell heights are conditional within columns. Weekly-only and episodic-only are different patterns, not an ordered severity scale. Areas are normalised only for published rounding.

title: State prevalence
question: How does risky-drinking prevalence differ among states and territories?
reading: Equal-sized tiles give small territories the same visibility as large states; colour shows percentage, not population size.
reason: A tile cartogram retains approximate geography while preventing large land areas from dominating the comparison.
alternative: A conventional Australian choropleth would give large states much more visual weight.
limitation: Tile positions are approximate. The fixed 0–60% scale encodes the selected survey population's percentage; counts and land area are not encoded.

title: Recorded treatment demand
question: Where are recorded alcohol treatment episodes concentrated geographically?
reading: Circle area compares episode counts at geographic locations; a fixed size scale keeps different years comparable.
reason: A proportional-symbol map combines location with the size of recorded caseload, contrasting with prevalence in the neighbouring chart.
alternative: Sorted bars would rank counts more precisely; exact labels and the size legend support comparison here.
limitation: Episodes are not unique clients or population-adjusted rates, and do not establish unmet demand. ACT's displaced circle is connected to its location.

title: Hospitalisations by age and sex
question: How do recorded hospitalisation counts differ by age group and sex?
reading: Paired bars share a zero baseline. Within each age group, male bars are above female bars.
reason: Grouped horizontal bars make positive counts directly comparable within age groups and leave room for exact count labels.
alternative: A mirrored pyramid introduces negative plotting positions and resembles a population structure despite uneven age bands.
limitation: Counts describe episodes, not unique people or age-specific risk. The open-ended 55+ group includes more ages; the national total includes categories outside these bars.

title: Disease burden contributions
question: Which listed disease groups contribute most to alcohol-attributable healthy life years lost?
reading: Ranked bar lengths make contributions easier to compare; the lighter bar is the explicitly labelled derived residual.
reason: Six groups fit on a shared zero baseline with readable names, counts and tooltip shares. Wider views also label the shares directly.
alternative: A treemap provides a composition overview, but comparing areas and fitting labels is less effective for this ranking question.
limitation: The residual is the total minus the five listed groups, not an invented disease category. The same count scale is used for every selected sex; colour identifies listed values versus the residual.

title: Mortality changes over time
question: How did yearly increases and decreases add up to the difference between 2015 and 2024?
reading: Floating bars explain how signed yearly changes add up; the final column is the 2024 total, not another change.
reason: A waterfall makes the arithmetic contribution of each year's change explicit while retaining the starting and ending totals.
alternative: A line would show the trajectory, but would not separate the contributions to the final difference as directly.
limitation: Increases and decreases explain the arithmetic, not its causes. Recent counts can be revised; alcohol-induced deaths are narrower than all alcohol-attributable deaths.
